title: Say You'll Haunt Me: A Ghost Story About Ed

content:
I don't usually write about personal things on this blog, but I'm  trying something different this month. Here's a ghost story about my friend Ed. Although I consider myself something of a skeptic, he believed firmly in life after death. Ed, this one's for you!

I met Ed on March 25, 1991. We were both volunteers at the AIDS Action Committee's Oscars Party, which was held at one of the big hotels in Boston's Copley Square. I was relatively new to the city and looking for community. One of Ed's friends had recently died from AIDS and he was looking to meet new people. I don't remember much about that party, but we decided to hang out later. 

Edward J. Martin, 1964 - 2017

We quickly became good friends. We would have boozy lunches at Whiskey's on Boylston Street, wander aimlessly through stores on Newbury Street, and see puzzling arthouse movies at the queer film festival. Ed also took my partner Tony and me to some very memorable parties.  

Ed was wilder than I was, so I played more of a supporting role in our youthful misadventures. Ed was always the star. Sometimes when we did bar outreach for AIDS Action Committee, older, dangerous-looking men flirted with Ed. "That mobster thought he could buy my affections for a pack of cigarettes," Ed said to me one night as we packed up our educational materials. "But I'm worth more than that!"

Late one rainy Halloween night, Ed and I wound up in Bay Village at Napoleon's, a gay piano bar. It was almost closing time, and we looked like drowned rats. Ed's vampire makeup was running down his face onto his costume. His wig was wet and matted. Despite this, a stone-faced man invited Ed (and me) back to his apartment in Allston to do some drugs. 

"I think he wants to kill us and eat us," Ed whispered to me, only half-joking. Wisely, he declined the invitation. Cannibalistic serial-killer Jeffrey Dahmer had only been caught the year before, and Ed wasn't taking any chances. 

In retrospect, I can see that Ed had a very bright spirit. All types of people - even potentially dangerous ones - were drawn to him because they could see that he loved life. Here are just a few things he loved: his family and friends, the playwright Tennessee Williams, Versace, hot weather, Provincetown and Cape Cod, good-looking men, and the Stoneholm. 

The Stoneholm, if you don't know it, is a large, historic apartment building on Beacon Street in Brookline. Built in a French Baroque style from granite, the Stoneholm is beautiful, impressive, and a little ominous. Ed used to live near it, and pointed it out to me once as we drove by. Eventually, I moved to that neighborhood and began passing it on my daily commute to the office. 

I always thought about Ed whenever I went by the Stoneholm. 

Ed developed cancer around 2004. The cancer was definitely hard for him, but he remained passionate about life, and got married and eventually moved to Florida. He hated winter and wanted to spend the rest of his life someplace warm. 

After living with cancer for 13 years, Ed died on October 26, 2017. His husband Bill called me from Florida that morning to tell me the news. I cried, and then I went to work.

My team was organizing a big conference that day so I had to work late. I took an Uber home, and the old Lionel Ritchie song "Say You, Say Me" was playing as we drove by the Stoneholm. I thought of Ed, and my eyes drifted to the car's dashboard. 

I glanced at the sound system's display panel. It read, "Say You'll Haunt Me." 

I looked again to make sure I wasn't misreading it. No, it still read "Say You'll Haunt Me," even though that wasn't the name of the song. My hair stood up on my head. Was this some kind of message from Ed? As I said earlier, I consider myself a skeptic, but if this was just a coincidence it was an uncanny one. 

I suppose it could have just been a technical glitch in Sirius or whatever music service the Uber driver was using. I did a Google search when I got home, and found that "Say You'll Haunt Me" is a song by the band Stone Sour. It includes these lyrics:

Say you want to stay you want me too

Say you'll never die, you'll always haunt me

I want to know I belong to you

Say you'll haunt me

A couple nights later, I dreamt about Ed. I was in some kind of underground shopping mall, and he was walking down the stairs into it from the outside. He was youthful, and radiated wild energy. There was something fiery about him, as if all his mortal parts and physical limitations had been burned away. 

It was very intense, and I woke up abruptly. Later, I called his husband Bill to tell him about the weird experience in the Uber and my dream. He was happy to hear these things had happened. 

"It was definitely Ed trying to talk to you," he said. "I've had some things happening here in Florida, too. Before he died, Ed told me he'd make the Christmas lights flash on this tree we have in our living room if he could. When I came home after he died at the hospital, the lights began to flash." 

*****

Well, that's my ghost story about Ed. I still miss him. Some folklorists and historians say ghost stories are a way for communities to remember past events. When we tell ghost stories, we recount events that happened so future generations to remember them. His husband Bill passed away this summer, so I'm writing this as a way of remembering both of them. 

This ghost story also shows that weird things often happen when people die, even to skeptics who don't necessarily believe in ghosts.
